title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
subtitle: How transport protocols evolved from serialized TCP sockets to binary multiplexing and finally QUIC over UDP.
keyTakeaways: HTTP/1.1 suffered from application-level head-of-line blocking because requests on a single TCP connection had to be answered sequentially.
HTTP/2 solved application head-of-line blocking via binary stream multiplexing over a single TCP socket, but introduced transport-level blocking when single packets drop.
HTTP/3 eliminates transport head-of-line blocking entirely by replacing TCP with QUIC over UDP, giving each stream independent loss recovery and zero-RTT reconnection.
architectureDiagram:
HTTP/1.1: [ Req 1 ] -> [ Resp 1 ] -> [ Req 2 ] -> [ Resp 2 ] (Serialized)

HTTP/2:   [ Stream 1: Chunk A ][ Stream 2: Chunk A ][ Stream 1: Chunk B ] (TCP Stream)
          (Dropping one TCP packet halts all active streams)

HTTP/3:   [ Stream 1 (UDP) ]    [ Stream 2 (UDP) ]    [ Stream 3 (UDP) ]
          (Dropping a packet on Stream 1 does not affect Stream 2)

sections.heading: From HTTP/1.1 Queuing to HTTP/2 Multiplexing
sections.body: HTTP/1.1 formats messages as human-readable text and requires a response to complete before the next request can be sent on that socket. Browsers worked around this head-of-line blocking by opening up to six concurrent TCP connections per domain. HTTP/2 fundamentally changed this by replacing plaintext with binary framing: headers and data are broken into frames stamped with stream IDs, allowing hundreds of concurrent requests and responses to interleave over a single TCP connection.
bullets: Binary Framing: Replaces ASCII parsing with compact binary frames, cutting parsing overhead and syntax ambiguity.
Stream Multiplexing: Eliminates the need for multiple TCP sockets, connection keep-alive pools, and domain sharding hacks.
HPACK Header Compression: Uses a shared dynamic table to compress redundant HTTP headers across subsequent requests on the same connection.

codeSnippet.title: Stream Multiplexing Mechanics Across Generations
codeSnippet.code:
/*
 * HTTP/1.1:
 * Socket 1: [ GET /index.html ] -> [ 200 OK ] -> [ GET /style.css ] -> [ 200 OK ]
 * (If /index.html takes 500ms, /style.css waits behind it!)
 *
 * HTTP/2:
 * Single TCP Socket:
 * [ Frame: Stream 1 (HTML chunk 1) ]
 * [ Frame: Stream 3 (CSS chunk 1)  ]
 * [ Frame: Stream 1 (HTML chunk 2) ]
 * [ Frame: Stream 5 (Image chunk 1)]
 * (Interleaved concurrently!)
 *
 * The Catch in HTTP/2:
 * If packet containing [Stream 3: CSS chunk 1] drops on the network,
 * the OS TCP stack pauses ALL streams until that packet is retransmitted.
 */

sections.heading: HTTP/3 and QUIC: Eliminating TCP Head-of-Line Blocking
sections.body: While HTTP/2 solved application head-of-line blocking, it exposed TCP's transport-level head-of-line blocking. Because TCP enforces strict byte-stream ordering, if a single packet drops on a lossy cellular connection, the operating system kernel holds all subsequent bytes in memory until the missing packet is retransmitted—stalling every multiplexed HTTP/2 stream simultaneously. HTTP/3 solves this by operating over UDP using QUIC. In QUIC, each stream manages its own sequence numbers and flow control; dropping a packet on Stream 1 has zero impact on Streams 2 or 3.
bullets: Independent Packet Streams: Packet loss on one resource never halts unrelated assets.
Integrated 1-RTT Handshake: QUIC combines the transport handshake and TLS 1.3 cryptographic negotiation into a single round trip (0-RTT on reconnects).

Connection Migration: Connections are tracked by a 64-bit Connection ID rather than the 4-tuple of IP/Port, allowing mobile devices to switch seamlessly between Wi-Fi and 5G without dropping active downloads.

tradeOffs.pros: Mature tooling, universal corporate firewall support; excellent throughput over stable, low-loss datacenter networks.
tradeOffs.cons: Suffers severe throughput degradation on lossy mobile networks due to TCP head-of-line blocking and slow-start retransmits.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal microservice RPC meshes (gRPC), server-to-server communications, and enterprise LANs.

tradeOffs.pros: Immune to transport head-of-line blocking; instantaneous connection migration on mobile networks; fastest connection setup.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher CPU utilization on edge servers for UDP packet processing; some corporate firewalls block outbound UDP traffic on port 443.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Public-facing mobile apps, streaming media, edge CDN delivery, and interactive web client traffic.

interviewTip: When asked why HTTP/3 moved to UDP, don't just say 'because UDP is faster.' Explain that TCP guarantees in-order byte delivery, so a dropped packet halts all multiplexed streams in the kernel. HTTP/3 moves reliability into user-space streams over UDP so packet loss on one stream doesn't stall others.
